cards.front: Why is it useful to a cell that microtubule ends grow and collapse by themselves?
cards.back: Ends can search the cell interior, the ones that find a target can be kept, and the array can be rebuilt quickly when the cell changes shape or divides.
cards.quote: Ends that grow and collapse by themselves let a microtubule array search the cell interior, keep the ends that find a target

cards.front: Rank actin filaments, intermediate filaments and microtubules by width, with approximate values.
cards.back: Actin filament about 7 nm < intermediate filament about 10 nm < microtubule about 25 nm (a hollow tube of usually 13 protofilaments).
cards.quote: about 25 nm, a hollow tube of (usually) 13 protofilaments
cards.section: Three polymers built for different jobs

cards.front: Which nucleotide does each cytoskeletal polymer bind: actin filaments, microtubules, intermediate filaments?
cards.back: Actin: ATP. Microtubules: GTP. Intermediate filaments: none, and they have no enzyme activity.
cards.quote: Intermediate filaments, with no nucleotide and one kind of end, are the contrast case
cards.section: Three polymers built for different jobs

cards.front: Name the intermediate-filament protein typical of fibroblasts and the family typical of epithelial cells.
cards.back: Vimentin in fibroblasts; keratins in epithelial cells. Both are fibrous proteins.
cards.quote: fibrous proteins (vimentin in fibroblasts, keratins in epithelial cells)
cards.section: Three polymers built for different jobs

cards.front: Why does a microtubule have a plus end and a minus end?
cards.back: α/β-tubulin dimers stack head to tail into protofilaments, and every dimer points the same way, so the two ends differ. β-tubulin is exposed at the plus end.
cards.quote: Every dimer points the same way, so the tube has a plus end and a minus end.
cards.section: Three polymers built for different jobs

cards.front: Why do cytoplasmic intermediate filaments such as vimentin lack structural polarity?
cards.back: Two coiled-coil dimers line up antiparallel and half staggered to form the tetramer, so the building block points both ways and the filament's ends match.
cards.quote: two coiled-coil dimers line up antiparallel and half staggered to form a tetramer, and a building block that points both ways gives a filament with no polarity
cards.section: Three polymers built for different jobs

cards.front: Intermediate filaments are the most flexible of the three polymers in bending. Does that make them weak?
cards.back: No. A single filament can be stretched beyond two or three times its resting length without breaking. Bending and stretching are different tests, like a rope beside a fishing rod.
cards.quote: Intermediate filaments are the most flexible in bending, yet a single filament can be stretched beyond two or three times its resting length without breaking.
cards.section: Three polymers built for different jobs

cards.front: In comparisons of purified filaments, which cytoskeletal polymer is stiffest in bending, and what does that suit it for?
cards.back: The microtubule. Its stiffness suits it to serve as tracks and struts.
cards.quote: microtubules are the stiffest in bending, which suits them to serve as tracks and struts
cards.section: Three polymers built for different jobs

cards.front: How do cells take intermediate filaments apart, and what is the standard example?
cards.back: By phosphorylation; the nuclear lamins are disassembled this way at mitosis.
cards.quote: cells take them apart by phosphorylation, as with the nuclear lamins at mitosis
cards.section: Three polymers built for different jobs

cards.front: The critical concentration of a filament end is Cc = {{c1::koff / kon}}, the free subunit concentration at which subunits join the end as fast as they leave.
cards.back: Above Cc the end grows; below it the end shrinks.
cards.quote: Each filament end, in a given state, has a critical concentration, Cc = koff / kon: the free subunit concentration at which subunits join the end as fast as they leave.
cards.section: Three polymers built for different jobs

cards.front: How does nucleotide hydrolysis after assembly give a cytoskeletal polymer two kinds of end?
cards.back: Old subunits hold on less tightly. An end with fresh nucleotide is tight (low Cc); an end exposing old nucleotide is loose (high Cc).
cards.why: Between the two Ccs the polymer cannot come to rest with nothing moving.
cards.quote: Hydrolysis after assembly makes old subunits hold on less tightly, so a polymer gets two kinds of end.
cards.section: Three polymers built for different jobs

cards.front: Treadmilling and dynamic instability both come from tight and loose ends. How do actin filaments and microtubules arrange the two kinds differently?
cards.back: Actin puts them at its two ends at once, a difference in space: treadmilling. A microtubule end switches between them over time, growing while capped with GTP and collapsing when uncapped: dynamic instability.
cards.quote: Actin puts the two kinds at its two ends, so it treadmills: the difference is in space.
cards.section: Three polymers built for different jobs

cards.front: The critical-concentration rule applies to single ends with purified proteins. Name two things it does not tell you.
cards.back: The rates in a cell, where accessory proteins (profilin, formins, cofilin, capping protein, EB proteins) change them, some by an order of magnitude or more; and when a capped end will lose its cap.
cards.quote: It says whether a polymer can settle and which way each end moves, not the rates in a cell
cards.section: Three polymers built for different jobs

cards.front: Tubes of pure actin at a range of total concentrations are left to settle, and free actin is plotted against total actin. Describe the plot and how it gives the critical concentration.
cards.back: Below a certain total nothing polymerizes, so free actin rises in step with total. Above it, free actin stays flat and every extra subunit goes into polymer. For a polymer with one Cc, the flat level, which is also the total where the line bends, is Cc; for real ATP-actin, whose two ends differ, it settles between the two ends' values.
cards.quote: The flat level of free actin is the critical concentration, Cc, and it is also the total where the line bends.
cards.section: One end: the doorway and its critical concentration

cards.front: Why does polymerization of pure actin or tubulin begin with a lag phase, and how do cells use that?
cards.back: Starting a filament is hard: a few subunits must come together before an end exists. So cells control where filaments start, with formins and the Arp2/3 complex for actin and γ-tubulin at the centrosome for microtubules.
cards.quote: The lag is there because starting a filament is hard: a few subunits must come together before an end exists.
cards.section: One end: the doorway and its critical concentration

cards.front: Treating a filament end as a doorway, why does free subunit concentration stop at one value, Cc?
cards.back: Arrival is proportional to free concentration C (kon × C) while departure (koff) does not depend on C. Net growth kon × C − koff is zero only at C = koff/kon.
cards.quote: Subunits arrive at a rate proportional to the free subunit concentration C, and leave at a rate that does not depend on C.
cards.section: One end: the doorway and its critical concentration

cards.front: A filament end has kon = 4 per µM per s and koff = 2 per s. What is its critical concentration, and what does the end do at 2 µM free subunit?
cards.back: Cc = koff/kon = 2/4 = 0.5 µM. At 2 µM: 4 × 2 − 2 = +6 subunits per s, so the end grows.
cards.why: Free concentration is above Cc, so gain beats loss.
cards.quote: At 10 µM tubulin: 8.9 × 10 − 44 = 89 − 44 = +45 dimers per s, so the end grows.
cards.section: One end: the doorway and its critical concentration

cards.front: A tube holds 3 µM total of a subunit whose filament ends all share one Cc of 0.5 µM. At steady state, how much is free and how much is in polymer?
cards.back: Free = Cc = 0.5 µM; polymer = 3 − 0.5 = 2.5 µM.
cards.why: Any free subunit above Cc joins filament ends until gain and loss match again.
cards.quote: Any free actin above Cc joins filament ends until gain and loss match again.
cards.section: One end: the doorway and its critical concentration

cards.front: Imagine actin that never hydrolysed its ATP. Could its barbed end have a lower critical concentration than its pointed end? What measured case supports the answer?
cards.back: No. Adding a subunit at either end gives the same filament one subunit longer, so the energy change and the ratio koff/kon are the same. ADP-actin, which cannot hydrolyse further, has end Ccs of about 1.9 and 1.7 µM, equal within error.
cards.why: The barbed end can be faster at both adding and losing, but not at one alone.
cards.quote: The energy change is the same, so the balance point, koff/kon, must be the same.
cards.section: Two ends: why hydrolysis makes them differ

cards.front: In actin's nucleotide cycle within the filament, which step loosens a subunit: ATP hydrolysis or phosphate release?
cards.back: Phosphate release. Hydrolysis by itself barely loosens a subunit.
cards.quote: Hydrolysis by itself barely loosens a subunit; release of the phosphate does.
cards.section: Two ends: why hydrolysis makes them differ

cards.front: In the standard simplified picture, why is the actin barbed end a tight end and the pointed end a loose end?
cards.back: The barbed end grows fast, so fresh ATP-actin arrives before tip subunits hydrolyse: low Cc. The pointed end adds slowly and, in the treadmilling window, loses subunits, exposing older ADP-actin that has released phosphate: higher Cc.
cards.quote: The barbed end grows fast, so new ATP-actin keeps arriving before the subunits there have hydrolysed.
cards.section: Two ends: why hydrolysis makes them differ

cards.front: Purified ATP-actin filaments have Cc about 0.1 µM at the barbed end and about 0.6 µM at the pointed end. What does each end do if free ATP-actin is held at 0.4 µM? At 2 µM?
cards.back: At 0.4 µM (between the two Ccs): barbed end grows, pointed end shrinks. At 2 µM (above both): both ends grow, the barbed end faster.
cards.why: Each end grows above its own Cc and shrinks below it; only the window between them gives opposite behaviour.
cards.quote: At 0.3 µM, between them: the barbed end grows and the pointed end shrinks.
cards.section: Two ends: why hydrolysis makes them differ

cards.front: For ATP-actin, barbed end kon = 11.6 per µM per s, koff = 1.4 per s; pointed end kon = 1.3, koff = 0.8. Where does free actin settle at steady state, and why is it near the barbed-end Cc?
cards.back: (1.4 + 0.8)/(11.6 + 1.3) = 2.2/12.9 ≈ 0.17 µM. It is a kon-weighted average of the two Ccs (0.12 and 0.62 µM), and the barbed end's about ninefold larger kon pulls it close to 0.12.
cards.quote: The steady-state concentration, (1.4 + 0.8)/(11.6 + 1.3) ≈ 0.17 µM, is an average of the two critical concentrations weighted by each end's kon.
cards.section: Checking the rule against measured constants

cards.front: What is treadmilling of an actin filament?
cards.back: At steady state the filament's length holds steady while subunits join at the barbed end, age along the filament and leave at the pointed end.
cards.why: Binding drives assembly; hydrolysis afterwards turns the steady state into a flux.
cards.quote: Now the filament's length holds steady while subunits flow through it, joining at the barbed end, aging along the filament and leaving at the pointed end.
cards.section: Two ends: why hydrolysis makes them differ

cards.front: In microtubule dynamic instability, what are a catastrophe and a rescue?
cards.back: A catastrophe is an end's switch from steady growth to rapid shortening; a rescue is the switch back to growth.
cards.quote: The switch to shortening is a catastrophe; the switch back is a rescue.
cards.section: One end, two states: dynamic instability

cards.front: Explain the GTP cap model of microtubule dynamic instability.
cards.back: Dimers join with GTP on β-tubulin, which is hydrolysed soon after inside the lattice. GDP-tubulin stays in the straight lattice only while a cap of unhydrolysed dimers remains; capped ends grow, uncapped ends shed dimers fast.
cards.quote: GDP-tubulin is held in the straight lattice only by its neighbours; the end stays intact while a cap of not-yet-hydrolysed dimers remains.
cards.section: One end, two states: dynamic instability

cards.front: Why does a microtubule end peel apart once it loses its GTP cap?
cards.back: GDP-tubulin protofilaments are curved. Without the cap holding them straight side by side, they curl outward from the end, like bent plastic strips released from a clamp.
cards.quote: GDP-tubulin protofilaments are curved in the same way, and once the cap is gone they curl outward.
cards.section: One end, two states: dynamic instability

cards.front: Name two ways a microtubule end can lose its GTP cap, and explain why catastrophes are random events.
cards.back: By chance, or because addition slows and hydrolysis catches up. A cap can be lost by chance even at a steady growth rate, so catastrophes are random.
cards.quote: The cap can be lost by chance, or because addition slows and hydrolysis catches up.
cards.section: One end, two states: dynamic instability

cards.front: A tubulin mutant hydrolyses its GTP more slowly after joining a microtubule. Predict the effect on cap length and on how often growing ends undergo catastrophe.
cards.back: Longer cap, as recombinant human tubulin mutants showed. By the cap model (not shown in the lesson for these mutants), a bigger cap should be harder to lose, so catastrophes should become rarer.
cards.why: In the cap model, the cap is the region not yet hydrolysed; the end is tight while it remains.
cards.quote: Slowing hydrolysis lengthens the cap, as recombinant human tubulin mutants show
cards.section: One end, two states: dynamic instability

cards.front: A purified microtubule end has lost its cap and is shortening rapidly. Free tubulin is raised from 8 to 15 µM. Does the shortening slow?
cards.back: Barely. The uncapped end's critical concentration is by a rough estimate far above any tested tubulin level, so more tubulin cannot turn loss into gain. Purified pig brain tubulin showed shortening rate unchanged over 7 to 15.5 µM.
cards.quote: rapid shortening did not change with tubulin concentration over 7 to 15.5 µM
cards.section: One end, two states: dynamic instability

cards.front: Free tubulin is raised for growing purified pig brain microtubules (1988 study). Predict the effect on catastrophe frequency and give the cap-model reason.
cards.back: Catastrophes become rarer. A capped end grows faster with more tubulin and is thought to build a bigger cap that is harder to lose.
cards.why: The cap model fits this, though catastrophe also depends on the age of the end.
cards.quote: that more tubulin made catastrophes rarer at both ends
cards.section: One end, two states: dynamic instability

cards.front: Purified microtubules are dynamic at both ends. What often happens to minus ends in cells?
cards.back: They are often capped or anchored, for example at the centrosome.
cards.quote: In cells, minus ends are often capped or anchored, for example at the centrosome.
cards.section: One end, two states: dynamic instability

cards.front: A purified microtubule plus end grows 3 µm in 90 s, then shortens 3 µm in 6 s. Give growth and shortening velocities in µm per min and their ratio.
cards.back: Growth: 3 µm / 1.5 min = 2 µm per min. Shortening: 3 µm / 6 s = 0.5 µm per s = 30 µm per min. Shortening is 15 times faster.
cards.quote: Step 2, shortening velocity. 6.0 µm in 12 s = 0.5 µm per s = 30 µm per min, twenty times faster than growth.
cards.section: A worked problem: reading one trace

cards.front: A microtubule end spends 600 s growing in total with 3 catastrophes, and 20 s shortening in total with 1 rescue. Give the catastrophe frequency per min and the rescue frequency per s.
cards.back: Catastrophe: 3 / 600 s = 0.005 per s = 0.3 per min. Rescue: 1 / 20 s = 0.05 per s.
cards.why: Each frequency is switches divided by time spent in the state being left.
cards.quote: Each frequency is the number of switches divided by the time spent in the state they leave.
cards.section: A worked problem: reading one trace

cards.front: Assume 13 protofilaments and 8 nm per tubulin dimer. How many dimers per second does a plus end add when growing at 2 µm per min?
cards.back: 1 µm = 1,000/8 = 125 dimers per protofilament × 13 = 1,625 dimers. 2 µm per min = 0.0333 µm per s × 1,625 ≈ 54 dimers per s.
cards.quote: so one micrometre holds 1,000 nm ÷ 8 nm = 125 dimers per protofilament, and 125 × 13 = 1,625 dimers in all.
cards.section: A worked problem: reading one trace

cards.front: HeLa cells are treated with taxol at 5 nM and, separately, at a much higher dose. Predict the effect on microtubule polymer mass and dynamics at each dose.
cards.back: Low dose: HeLa polymer mass does not rise (below 10 nM); damped growth and shortening, so the sawtooth flattens, was shown with purified brain microtubules. Higher doses: microtubules are stabilized and extra polymer is added.
cards.why: Taxol binds β-tubulin in the assembled lattice, including old GDP-tubulin behind the cap.
cards.quote: In HeLa cells, taxol did not raise microtubule polymer mass below 10 nM but did at higher doses
cards.section: Drug effects that depend on the system

cards.front: Colchicine binds free tubulin dimers. How does that block microtubule growth?
cards.back: The drug-dimer complex adds to a microtubule end and blocks further growth there. Small amounts suppress dynamics.
cards.quote: the drug-dimer complex adds to an end and blocks further growth there
cards.section: Drugs as tests

cards.front: Cultured newt lung epithelial cells are treated with nanomolar nocodazole (4 to 400 nM). Predict the effect on their microtubules, and say what the lesson reports for micromolar doses.
cards.back: Nanomolar (4 to 400 nM): microtubules pause and both growth and shortening slow. Micromolar doses, as commonly used on cultured mammalian cells, remove most microtubules; the lesson gives no micromolar result for newt lung cells.
cards.why: The effect depends on dose and cell type.
cards.quote: the micromolar doses common on cultured mammalian cells remove most of them
cards.section: Drugs as tests

cards.front: Phalloidin binds along actin filaments and slows disassembly. Why is fluorescent phalloidin used mainly on fixed cells?
cards.back: It enters living cells poorly, so it serves mainly as a stain for actin filaments after fixation.
cards.quote: enters living cells poorly, so fluorescent phalloidin mainly stains filaments in fixed cells
cards.section: Drugs as tests

cards.front: Cytochalasin B binding was measured on actin-coated beads while the number of filament ends was varied and total actin held constant. Binding tracked the number of ends. What does this show, and what does it not show?
cards.back: It shows cytochalasin B binds filament ends rather than actin generally. It does not by itself show which end; that it is the barbed end came from other experiments.
cards.quote: That experiment shows end binding; it does not by itself show which end.
cards.section: Drug effects that depend on the system

cards.front: Latrunculin A is added to purified actin at steady state. Predict the effect on polymer amount and explain the main mechanism, with its caveat.
cards.back: Polymer falls. Latrunculin A binds actin monomers 1:1 and sequesters them, so fewer free subunits can join ends. Caveat: it also speeds disassembly at the ends of fresh ATP-actin filaments, so sequestration is not the whole story.
cards.quote: sequesters them (holds them so they cannot join), lowering polymer
cards.section: Drugs as tests

cards.front: One lab reports that nanomolar nocodazole (4 to 400 nM) makes microtubule catastrophes more frequent in newt lung epithelial cells; another finds them less frequent in BSC-1 monkey kidney cells after an hour. Is one result wrong?
cards.back: Not necessarily. The other effects were similar in both systems; the direction of one switching parameter depends on the system. State dose and system with any drug effect.
cards.quote: So the direction of one switching parameter depends on the system.
cards.section: Drug effects that depend on the system

cards.front: You want to test whether vimentin filaments are needed for a fibroblast behaviour. Why is withaferin A a weak test, and what is better?
cards.back: Withaferin A redistributes vimentin in human fibroblasts but is not selective and did not alter assembly of purified vimentin. Removing vimentin genetically and then adding it back is cleaner.
cards.quote: removing vimentin genetically and then adding it back is the cleaner test
cards.section: Drugs as tests

cards.front: Total actin fluorescence in a fibroblast lamellipodium is constant over 5 minutes. Why can't that tell static filaments from treadmilling ones, and how would you decide?
cards.back: A treadmilling network and a static one can hold the same polymer. Mark part of it (bleach a stripe, photoactivate a patch, or sparse speckles), image every few seconds while the edge holds still, and follow the mark.
cards.quote: A treadmilling network and a static one can hold the same polymer.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A stripe of fluorescent actin is bleached across a stationary lamellipodium. Interpret three outcomes: the mark moves rearward; the mark stays put and does not recover; the mark recovers in place without moving.
cards.back: Rearward movement (with new fluorescence at the front): the network flows back while new network is added in front, as in treadmilling. Stays put, no recovery: static filaments. Recovers in place: exchange all along the filaments.
cards.quote: Exchange all along the filaments: the mark recovers in place without moving.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In a photobleaching experiment on lamellipodial actin, what controls are needed, and what should each show?
cards.back: A fixed cell: the mark neither moves nor recovers. An unbleached region: measures bleaching by imaging alone. Jasplakinolide, which stabilizes actin filaments: should slow the mark.
cards.quote: Controls: a fixed cell, where the mark should neither move nor recover
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Suppose a tubulin variant joins microtubules with GTP but can never hydrolyse it. Using the critical-concentration rule, predict whether microtubules made of it would show dynamic instability.
cards.back: No. Without hydrolysis there is no loose, old-nucleotide end state, so every end shares one Cc and the polymer simply settles, growing above Cc and shrinking below it without switching.
cards.why: The rule: hydrolysis after assembly is what creates two kinds of end.
cards.quote: If subunits never hydrolysed their nucleotide, every end of a polymer would share one Cc, and the polymer would simply settle.
cards.section: Three polymers built for different jobs

cards.front: Would you expect vimentin intermediate filaments to treadmill or show dynamic instability? Reason from the critical-concentration rule.
cards.back: Neither. They bind no nucleotide and, being apolar, have one kind of end, so the rule predicts no treadmilling or instability. They still exchange subunits slowly and are disassembled by phosphorylation.
cards.quote: the rule predicts neither treadmilling nor instability
cards.section: Three polymers built for different jobs

cards.front: Combine the GTP cap model with taxol's binding site: why should low-dose taxol suppress microtubule shortening even though it does not add polymer?
cards.back: One plausible reading, not shown in the lesson: shortening happens when an uncapped end's GDP-tubulin lattice comes apart. Taxol binds the assembled lattice, including GDP-tubulin behind the cap, so it may steady the very region that peels, damping shortening events.
cards.why: Rests on the cap model plus taxol binding β-tubulin in the lattice; no new mechanism added.
cards.quote: Taxol binds the assembled lattice, including the old GDP-tubulin behind the cap.
cards.section: Drugs as tests
